Welcome to Day 3 of Medical Lien Balance Verification Training. Today we build on what you already know about verifying balances. We will look at the entities that can place a lien on a client's claim, how to spot and handle duplicate liens, how to use ChartSwap to get lien documents, and then we will close with a summary and key takeaways. Keep your questions coming as we go, because every one of these topics shows up on real settled files.

Here is our roadmap for today. First, the entities involved, meaning everyone who can place a lien on a client's claim. Second, duplicate liens, where more than one party claims the same bill. Third, ChartSwap, the platform we use to request and download records, bills and lien documents. Finally, a summary and key takeaways that pull the whole lien balance verification training together. As we go, think about which of these you have already seen on a file.

Part one is about the entities involved. Before you can verify a balance, you need to know who is actually claiming money from the settlement and why. Each type of lienholder has its own basis for the claim, and that shapes who you contact and what you ask for. Let's go through them one at a time.

Now we cover who can place a lien on a claim. Several types of entities can hold a lien, and each one represents a legal right to a portion of the settlement for services rendered or costs incurred. Knowing who the lienholder is shapes who you contact and what documents you request. For example, a provider lien and a lien owned by a funding company are verified with different parties. Ask the group to name as many types of lienholders as they can before we go through them.

First, medical providers. Doctors, chiropractors and other professionals who treated the client on a lien basis can claim reimbursement from the settlement. Treating on lien means the client did not pay upfront, and the provider waits for the case to resolve. These are among the most common liens a Closing Specialist sees. For example, a chiropractor who treated the client for months after the accident will expect payment from the settlement. Ask trainees: why would a provider agree to wait for payment?

Next, hospitals. Hospitals can place liens for emergency care, surgeries and other treatment. Note the point on the slide: in some cases a hospital may place a lien even when health insurance covered part of the costs, depending on state law and specific agreements. That is exactly why we verify instead of assuming. A hospital lien may show the full billed charges while the insurer already paid a portion. Your job is to confirm what is actually owed and flag anything unusual to the attorney.

Health insurance companies can also place a lien. When they paid for the client's medical treatment, they may want those costs back from the settlement. The slide names this process: subrogation. It lets the insurer reclaim its expenses from the settlement when the third party is deemed liable. For you, this means the health plan is a lienholder like any other, and its balance needs to be confirmed in writing. Ask the group: where else have you heard the word subrogation?

Auto insurance companies are next. They may file a lien if they paid for medical bills or other related costs that must be reimbursed. In other words, if the client's own auto coverage paid something toward treatment, that carrier may expect to be repaid from the settlement. When you review the file, look for any payments made by an auto carrier so you know to ask whether a lien or reimbursement claim exists before funds go out.

Workers' compensation insurers come into play when the injury happened at work. If the workers' compensation insurance paid benefits, it may also place a lien on the claim to recover its costs. So whenever a file mentions a work injury or a workers' compensation claim, treat that carrier as a possible lienholder. Make sure its balance is part of your verification, so it is not discovered late, right before disbursement.

Government programs are another source of liens. In some cases, governmental programs or public assistance entities that provided aid, such as Medicare or Medicaid, may file a lien for reimbursement. If the client received benefits through one of these programs for accident-related care, expect a reimbursement claim. Note whether the client is covered by Medicare or Medicaid early in the file so these claims are identified and verified with everything else.

Third-party lien funders are private companies that provide loans or cash advances for medical bills or legal fees in exchange for a claim against the settlement. They are not the treating provider, so their paperwork and balances look different. Always get a current figure in writing close to disbursement. A common mistake is paying the provider directly when the right to payment actually belongs to the funder. Next, we look at duplicate liens, where this often matters.

Part two is duplicate liens. We will walk through a real example in the case management system where a lien is handled by a company other than the provider, and then go step by step through how to check for duplicate liens and make sure only the legitimate lienholder gets paid.

Let's take First Physical Therapy as an example. On the screen you see the client account in the case management system, and the arrow shows where to click the Medical Provider tab. This is illustrated using Filevine, so the screens may look different depending on the firm's CMS, but the idea is the same. Open the client account, go to the providers, and find the provider whose lien you are verifying.

When you open the provider, the contact details and the lien handler are displayed. Look at the two arrows. The provider is First Physical Therapy, but another entity is listed in the lien holder field. That tells us an additional company is involved, and we need to clarify all aspects before we rely on any balance. Again, this is illustrated in Filevine and may vary with the firm's CMS.

In this example, the liens are handled by RDG Holdings, LLC instead of the facility itself. This happens when a medical provider sells its invoices, transferring its right to reimbursement to a third party such as a lienholder or medical finance company. Practically, the verification request goes to that company, not the clinic. Ask the group: if the clinic says the account is zero, does that mean nothing is owed? Not necessarily, because the balance may now sit with the funder.

Here is the RDG Holdings contact card in the CMS, with its phone, email and address. Before you reach out, have the case details and lien information ready, including any relevant documentation. That way, when you contact the lienholder, you can identify the client, the provider and the dates of service right away. As before, this is shown in Filevine and may look different in your firm's CMS.

Why do providers sell their invoices? This approach is frequently seen in personal injury claims, or any case where immediate payment isn't possible. The third party establishes a lien on the patient's settlement or judgment and essentially waits for payment from the lawsuit's proceeds. For you, that means the company holding the lien may not be the one who treated the client, and it is the one you must verify with.

Now duplicate liens. Sometimes the same medical bill gets sold to more than one party, and you end up with two lienholders claiming the same services. There should only be one valid lienholder for any given set of services. If we pay both, the client's net is reduced twice for the same treatment. Watch for liens with the same dates of service and similar amounts from different companies. Ask trainees: what would make you suspect a duplicate?

When you suspect duplicates, request lien documentation from every claimant. That means the lien agreement, proof of assignment from the medical provider, and any supporting filings or notices. Then compare the dates and details side by side. If one assignment is dated before another, or the dates of service only partly overlap, those inconsistencies tell you where to dig. Do not decide who is valid on your own; document the conflict and escalate it.

Next, go back to the source. Contact the original medical provider and ask them to confirm who the debt was assigned to. Clarify whether multiple lienholders were assigned or whether it was an administrative error. The provider's confirmation, in writing, is what lets us pay only the legitimate lienholder. Ask the group: why is the provider the best party to settle a duplicate dispute?

If you can, get a copy of the original medical billing statement and compare it against the lien claims. The billing statement shows the actual services and invoices, so you can see whether two lienholders are pursuing the same bills. Each lien should line up with a distinct service or invoice. If two claims point to the same line items, you have found a likely duplicate to raise with the attorney.

Also review existing settlement agreements or lien resolutions to confirm that no prior lienholder has already been paid. A duplicate lienholder may have already been compensated, and that would invalidate its current claim. In practice, check the file for earlier resolutions or payments before you treat any new claim as owed. Paying a claim that was already satisfied comes straight out of the client's net.

Some duplicate situations are complicated. When that happens, it may be essential to seek legal advice to find the most effective course of action. Legal assistance may be needed to contest invalid liens or to settle conflicts among competing lienholders. Your role is to gather the documents, lay out the conflict clearly and bring it to the attorney, not to decide the dispute yourself.

Finally, timing. Address duplicate lien issues as early as possible, ideally before settlement negotiations begin. A duplicate found at disbursement holds up the client's money while it gets sorted out. Found early, it avoids delays in the settlement process and helps make sure funds are distributed appropriately. Ask trainees: at what point in your own workflow could you first spot a possible duplicate?

Part three is ChartSwap. This is a platform you will use to request and download medical records, bills and lien documents. We will cover what it is, why it is useful, and then walk through the screens step by step, from logging in to saving the documents in the CMS.

ChartSwap is a secure, HIPAA-compliant platform for exchanging medical records, bills and related documents between requesting parties and healthcare providers. It streamlines records requests in insurance claims, personal injury cases and legal proceedings. Because it is HIPAA-compliant, it is a safe channel for protected health information. Some providers route requests through it rather than answering fax or email. Ask trainees whether they have seen ChartSwap requests in a file before.

ChartSwap also supports lien documents. When providers have placed liens on a settlement, they can upload bills or lien information, and law firms or lienholders can access and download them for verification. When you pull a document from the platform, it still goes through the same review: check the client, provider, dates and balance, then save it to the CMS. A common mistake is leaving it in your downloads folder.

Speed is the main benefit here. ChartSwap's cloud-based system gives electronic access to documents, so retrieval is quick and wait times are reduced. Records and bills are often needed urgently in claims and legal cases, and ChartSwap provides a direct, digital connection between the provider and the requester. For a Closing Specialist waiting on a final bill before disbursement, that can save days.

ChartSwap is widely used wherever medical records are requested often, such as personal injury law, insurance, and healthcare revenue cycle management. It improves transparency, compliance and efficiency in medical record exchanges. That matters for timely claims processing and case management. Part four is the summary. We will review the main ideas from the whole Lien Balance Verification training, from why verification matters to monitoring, documentation and calculations, and then finish with three key takeaways to carry into your daily work.

Throughout the Lien Balance Verification training, we have covered the critical procedures and strategies for managing and verifying medical liens. The goal of all of it is a smooth settlement process, where the client gets an accurate net and every lienholder is paid the right amount. Let's take a moment to pull the main ideas together before the takeaways.

Here we revisit the basics. A lien is a legal claim on part of the settlement, owed to healthcare providers before the client receives their net amount. Verification means getting the lienholder to confirm what is actually owed. That ensures accurate allocation of funds and protects both the client and the company from discrepancies. A common mistake is relying on an old bill amount from months ago. Ask the group: who gets paid first, the lienholders or the client?

This slide is about the client's bottom line. Every dollar of lien we pay comes out of the client's net, so an unverified lien can significantly reduce what they take home. Verification confirms each bill and lien is legitimate and accounted for. Picture a provider that was already paid by health insurance but still shows the full charge; without verification we could pay it twice. Ask trainees: what two problems does verification prevent? Overpayment and double payment.

Proper monitoring means keeping a separate tracker to cross-reference lien amounts and bills. Think of it as a backup check. If the primary system has an error or data goes missing, your tracker shows what was requested, what came back and what changed. That way you are always prepared if something goes wrong. Ask the group: what columns would you want in your own tracker?

Accuracy and consistency come from documenting every step. From the first contact with a lienholder to the confirmation of the balance, every action should be logged. That includes call logs, written communication and updates on the lien status, kept in a structured and organized way. If someone else picks up the file tomorrow, they should be able to see exactly where it stands.

Proper documentation gives you an audit trail. If an issue comes up during settlement, your notes show what actions were taken and what communications happened, and when. That is vital when a lienholder disputes a balance or when an error needs to be corrected. A note that says who you spoke to, the date and the amount confirmed is worth far more than a memory of a phone call.

As the case nears settlement, you sum up all the verified medical bills and liens. The correct amounts are deducted from the total settlement before the client receives their portion. The calculation should be transparent and accurate, so every party is paid appropriately and anyone reviewing it can follow the numbers. Use only verified figures here, never estimates or outdated balances.

First takeaway: accuracy is key. Accurate records and verified liens let settlements be processed smoothly and reduce the risk of disputes or overpayment. Every step we covered serves that goal. If you are ever unsure whether a number is current and confirmed in writing, treat it as unverified. Ask the group: what is one accuracy check you will add to your own routine this week?

Second takeaway: communication matters. Regular and clear communication with lienholders, healthcare providers and third-party handlers keeps the verification process moving. That means clear requests, timely follow-ups and written confirmation of phone calls. A polite follow-up with the exact account details often gets a faster response than a vague second request. Ask trainees: which of these three groups do you contact most often?

Final takeaway: preparedness. Keep a separate tracker and documentation for each case so you are always ready to resolve a discrepancy if something goes wrong. When a lienholder disputes a balance at closing, the person with the saved documents, the written confirmation and the tracker resolves it quickly. To wrap up, take questions before we move on.
